doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: The Bing Crosby album
summary: Gordon explains his Bing Crosby tribute album, growing from a Chicago record club listening to Crosby's early recordings.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Wouldn’t do too much of that. Tell me about what inspired you to do an album about the music of Bing Crosby?

Well when I lived in Chicago we used to have a little record club, fellows that I knew, and we’d get together at this guy’s house. And we’d listen to the old Louis Armstrong records, the “Hot Five”s and the “Hot Seven”s and all of the things he made with Luis Russell. But also we got interested in Bing Crosby’s singing because he had a very nice voice. And we used to like to listen to him in the early days, when he was with John Scott Trotter’s orchestra, making recordings for Decca and before that, the other labels. And we enjoyed Bing’s style of jazz. And we started listening to him, the old records, back in the 60s, and I’ve been listening to him in the 70s, 80s and 90s now, and I’ve built up quite a collection, and that’s the reason we recorded this album, because we wanted to get young guys that were interested in playing Bing Crosby music or Bing Crosby songs. And I think, in my mind for instance, I always had it in the back of my mind that Bing would be a great guy to record later on, maybe now or do some of his stuff now, in a jazz vein. It’s kind of like a tribute to him.
